title: Borrowing and what it costs
summary: Learn that borrowing has a cost and how to think before you borrow.

variants.markdown:
**English draft for R5 review.**

Ravi's friend lends him ₹1,000 for a school trip kit. Ravi agrees to return ₹1,100 next month. That extra ₹100 is the **cost of borrowing**, and in loans it is called **interest**.

Banks and lenders work the same way, only with bigger amounts and a written agreement. If a family borrows ₹10,000 at an assumed 12% a year, then after one year the interest is about ₹1,200. This rate is **an assumption for this example, not a promise**; real rates differ a lot.

A smart borrower asks three questions:

- **Need or want?** Is this essential?
- **Total cost:** how much will I repay in all?
- **Can I repay?** Do I have a steady way to pay back on time?

Borrowing is not wrong. A loan for study can help. But it must be repaid, so it pays to borrow only what you need and compare the total cost first.

Gullak uses virtual play money only.

questions.prompt: Ravi borrows ₹1,000 and returns ₹1,100. What is the extra ₹100?
questions.explanation: The extra amount paid for using someone's money is called interest.

questions.prompt: Which question helps before taking a loan?

options.text: How much will I repay in total?
Which friend has the most money?

questions.explanation: Knowing the total repayment shows the real cost of the loan.

questions.prompt: Which is the wisest approach to borrowing?

options.text: Borrow only what you need and can repay

questions.explanation: Borrowing only what is needed, and planning to repay, keeps the cost under control.
